title: Systems graphics
instruction: Draw our systems atlas’s mechanisms so a reader can follow them one connection at a time.

opener.caption: Loop R13 from our systems atlas, with the authority line that leaves it and the layer it reaches. Each letter marks one part of the grammar, and the list names the rule that sets it.

intro: A systems graphic draws a mechanism: what moves what, which way, and how sure our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, is of each step. It uses the atlas’s own parts. Variables are the quantities or conditions that can rise or fall, connections are the arrows between them, and loops are chains of connections that come back to where they started.

Chapter 13 sets how a connection carries its grade, its delay and its source. The rules here show how to read and combine those marks and how to place a reform on them, then work through mechanisms from the atlas as it records them.

groups.title: Reading a systems drawing
groups.line: Each mark in a systems drawing answers one question about the mechanism, and a reader can name every answer without color.

groups.title: Reforms on the drawing
groups.line: A reform turns red only where the atlas says it acts, and its two grades stay apart.

groups.title: Worked examples from the atlas
groups.line: Each example draws one mechanism from our systems atlas as the atlas records it, and shows what a reader can take from it.

groups.title: Interaction
groups.line: A control lets a reader move through what the atlas holds, one step or one reform at a time, and offers nothing the atlas does not hold.

rules.title: Draw mechanisms at one weight, and let width or size measure only with a key.
rule: A systems graphic draws how one change leads to another. Its variables, the quantities or conditions that can rise or fall, sit in labeled pills, and its connections run between them as arrows. It carries no axis and no scale. Every connection in a drawing takes one width, 2 px in a figure, and every variable takes one pill, sized only by its label, so neither can pass for an amount.

Give a line’s width or a shape’s area a quantity only when a defined measure stands behind it, and print the key beside the drawing. A drawing whose widths carry measured flows, such as dollars moving between budgets, is a chart, and chapter 14 sets its rules.

text: Our systems atlas records the direction and the evidence of each connection and gives no loop a size: “Loops show structure: the size of any effect comes from the studies attached to each connection, and no whole loop has a measured strength.” A thicker line or a larger pill would claim a strength the atlas never measured, and a reader would take it at its word.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s methods, its limits; design judgment

correct.caption: Loop B1a from our systems atlas, “Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism”, with both connections at 2 px and both variables in pills of one size. The line patterns carry the grades, and nothing in the drawing measures.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.1. The second step is three times as thick and one pill is larger, with no key, so the drawing claims sizes our systems atlas never measured.

specs.label: Line width
specs.value: One width in a drawing: 2 px in a figure, 3 px in a large drawing; only Rule 12.5’s red target draws heavier

specs.label: Pill
specs.value: 130 px wide on a 296 px drawing, wider where the variable’s title would take more than three rows, with 12 px inside each end; 44 px tall, or the title’s rows at 18 px plus 22; a 2 px outline

specs.label: Width or area as a quantity
specs.value: Only with a defined measure and a key beside the drawing

specs.label: Measured flows
specs.value: A chart, under chapter 14’s rules

builders: Draw every connection with the atlas build’s wire_marks at one width, and size each pill from its wrapped label, so a pill grows only to hold its words.

rules.title: Name each variable, its kind and what a higher value means.
rule: Our systems atlas defines a variable as “a quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall”. Draw each one as a pill holding its own title, the name on its record, in every drawing, a loop’s among them, so it carries one name wherever it appears. The first time a reader meets it, give its typed chip, its kind in words and the atlas’s own sentence on what a higher value means.

Of its 51 variables, 31 are stocks, amounts built up over time, and nine are flows, amounts per period. Six are conditions the atlas calls auxiliary, worked out from other variables. The other five are outside drivers, forces whose causes lie outside the model, and Rule 15.9 sets where they go.

text: A name alone leaves the direction open. Turnout could mean more voters or a smaller gap between groups, and only the atlas’s sentence settles it for Variable B5: “A higher value means turnout is more similar across income groups.” Once a reader knows which way is up, the sign on every connection into the variable can be read.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and model conventions; house rule H02

correct.caption: A stock, a flow and a condition from our systems atlas, each with its pill, its typed chip, its kind and the atlas’s sentence on what a higher value means.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.2. Variable B5 is cut to Turnout, with no kind and no sentence, so its minus sign reads as fewer voters. The atlas’s variable is equality of voter turnout, and the sign says the gap between income groups widens.

specs.label: Name
specs.value: The variable’s own title, for all 51, never the shorter label a loop’s record lists for a step

specs.label: Label
specs.value: 15 px, semibold, wrapped inside the pill with 12 px at each end

specs.label: Kind
specs.value: Stock, flow, condition or outside driver, in words, from the variable’s type and its plain description; where the two disagree, as for Variable D6, no kind, since the atlas lists the question for its next version

specs.label: Higher value
specs.value: The atlas’s sentence, quoted, where the reader meets the variable first

specs.label: Chip
specs.value: Variable and the ID, as Rule 13.9 sets

builders: Read the name, the kind and the higher-value sentence from the variable’s own record, and stop the build if a drawing prints the shorter label a loop’s record lists for it. Print the sentence as the atlas writes it.

rules.title: Read a plus or minus as the way two variables move together.
rule: Each causal connection joins two variables, the quantities or conditions that can rise or fall, and carries a sign tag. A plus means the two tend to move the same way, and a minus means they move in opposite directions, with the model’s other conditions held steady. The word beside the tag says it again: raises for a plus, lowers for a minus.

Our systems atlas states the rule in its conventions: “The sign on a connection gives direction only.” Print the atlas’s sentence “A positive sign does not mean a benefit.” in every key that shows a sign.

text: Readers bring the plus and minus of a ledger, where plus means gain. In the atlas a plus sits on harmful changes too: when hostility toward the other party rises, exposure to hostile content tends to rise, and that connection carries a plus.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and model conventions

correct.caption: Two connections from our systems atlas, each with its sign tag, its word and the atlas’s sentence on what its sign means, over a key that quotes the atlas on a positive sign.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.3. The key calls a plus a positive effect, so more exposure to hostile content reads as good news and stronger oversight reads as harm.

specs.label: Sign tag
specs.value: 14 px body and 6 px point, 16 px tall, with an 8 by 2 px sign, on a 2 px line (Rule 10.10)

specs.label: Word
specs.value: Raises for a plus, lowers for a minus, 15 px beside the tag

specs.label: Minus
specs.value: A true minus sign, −, wherever the sign prints as text

specs.label: Key
specs.value: “A positive sign does not mean a benefit.”, quoted from the atlas

specs.label: Authority
specs.value: No tag (Rule 15.5)

builders: Take the word from the sign alone, and print the connection’s own sentence on its sign where a reader needs the reading in full.

rules.title: Say in words when a connection carries money, information or ownership.
rule: Our systems atlas gives each connection a type. Most are causal: a change in one variable changes another. Others name what moves along the line: money on 17 of them, such as contributions or advertising revenue; information on nine, such as news coverage or a feed; and ownership on five, where one quantity is held inside another. Print the type in words before the verb, as in “money, lowers”, and in the key.
Line patterns carry the evidence grade (Rule 13.4), so a type takes no pattern, width or color of its own. Authority, the fifth type, takes its own mark (Rule 15.5).

text: Gray print and low color vision take away color first, and the patterns already have a job. A word survives both, and it tells a reader what a connection is about before they open its record.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1

correct.caption: Three connections from our systems atlas, one of each type that names what moves, each with its type in words before its verb and its line in its grade’s pattern.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.4. Color alone tells the three types apart. In gray print the money and ownership lines match, and the key cannot say which is which.

specs.label: Type word
specs.value: Money, information or ownership, before the verb and a comma: money, lowers

specs.label: Causal
specs.value: No type word; the verb alone

specs.label: Never
specs.value: A color, a width or a pattern for a type

specs.label: Authority
specs.value: Its own mark and word (Rule 15.5)

builders: Print the type from the connection’s record, and leave the word out for a causal connection.

rules.title: Draw authority with its open diamond and no sign, outside every loop.
rule: An authority connection shows that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. In our systems atlas’s words, “It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.” Draw it solid, end it in an open diamond, and print decides where a causal line prints its verb.
Keep it out of every loop drawing, even where it touches a variable the loop holds. All seven of the atlas’s authority connections are documented, and none sits in a loop.

text: A sign would claim to know how an enforcer or a legislature will use its power. The atlas records the power and leaves the choice open, and a reader who met a diamond inside a loop would count a decision as one more step that runs by itself.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and model conventions

correct.caption: Two authority connections from our systems atlas into one variable, each with its open diamond and the word decides, crossing from the core layer to the technology layer.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.5. The enforcers’ line takes an arrowhead, a minus and lowers, so it claims they will cut the use of pricing software. The atlas records only that they decide.

specs.label: End
specs.value: An open diamond, 14 by 11 px, in place of the arrowhead (Rule 10.10)

specs.label: Line
specs.value: Solid; every authority connection is documented

specs.label: Word
specs.value: Decides, where a causal line prints its verb, or once in a key where every line in the drawing is an authority connection (Rule 15.17)

specs.label: Sign
specs.value: None

specs.label: Loops
specs.value: None; the build stops if any loop lists an authority connection

builders: Draw it with wire_marks and its authority switch, which sets the diamond and leaves the tag off.

rules.title: Number a loop’s steps in order, and name it reinforcing or balancing.
rule: A loop is “a chain of causes that returns to its starting variable”, in our systems atlas’s words. Number its steps from the variable the atlas starts it at, in the atlas’s order. Give the loop its typed chip and name beside the drawing, and set its ID and its kind inside it: reinforcing, coded R, where the returning effect amplifies the first change, or balancing, coded B, where it pushes back.

The minus signs give the kind. An even count, zero included, makes a loop reinforcing, and an odd count makes it balancing, as on all 20 of the atlas’s loops with numbered steps. Either kind can help or harm, depending on which way it runs.

text: Numbers let a reader follow a loop in the atlas’s order, aloud or one step at a time on a stepper (Rule 18.22). The count lets anyone check the kind from the drawing alone, and it shows how two minus signs make a loop that feeds itself.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and loop records; design judgment

correct.caption: Two loops from our systems atlas, each with numbered steps, its number and kind inside it, a sentence that reads it aloud and its count of minus signs.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.6. Loop R10 lacks its step numbers, chip and kind, and the words inside it judge the loop. Its two minus signs make it reinforcing.

specs.label: Step number
specs.value: Bold, before the verb, from the atlas’s first connection: 1 raises

specs.label: Inside the loop
specs.value: The loop’s typed ID in bold, such as Loop R10, then reinforcing or balancing

specs.label: Kind check
specs.value: An even count of minus signs for reinforcing, odd for balancing; the build checks every numbered loop

specs.label: Read aloud
specs.value: One sentence that carries more or less around the loop and back to the start

builders: Number steps in the order of the loop’s own list of connections, and stop the build if a loop’s kind and its count of minus signs disagree.

rules.title: Say how a loop closes, apart from how strong its evidence is.
rule: Our systems atlas records how each loop closes, in one of three ways: every step a numbered connection; closed through a step graded hypothesis; or conceptual, a mechanism with no complete chain of numbered connections. Print the closure in words beside the loop’s grade. Draw a hypothesized step in dots, and each step of a conceptual loop as the hollow line of Rule 13.4, between thin pills, since its stations are not the atlas’s numbered variables.
Of the atlas’s 23 loops, 18 close through numbered connections, two close through a hypothesis and three are conceptual.

text: Closure and grade answer different questions. A conceptual loop can rest on strong research and still lack a chain a reader can trace, and a loop that closes through a hypothesis stays uncertain as a whole, as the atlas defines closure: “If any closing step is only a hypothesis, the whole loop stays uncertain.”
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and loop records

correct.caption: Loop R16, which closes through a hypothesis, and Loop B3, a conceptual loop, each with its closure in words beside its grade.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.7. Loop B3 is drawn with solid numbered steps, so it passes for a chain of connections. The atlas grades the mechanism well supported and gives it no numbered connection.

specs.label: Every step numbered
specs.value: The loop as Rule 15.6 draws it

specs.label: Closes through a hypothesis
specs.value: The closing step in dots, with these words beside the grade

specs.label: Conceptual
specs.value: Hollow lines with their signs, 1 px pills, no step numbers or chips; “No numbered chain” beside the grade

specs.label: Counts
specs.value: 18 closed, two through a hypothesis, three conceptual, as of the snapshot

builders: Read the closure from the loop’s record, and draw a conceptual loop’s steps from its own list of stations and signs, since it lists no connections.

rules.title: Draw an open chain from start to end, and carry its sign along.
rule: An open chain is a run of connections that does not return to its start, such as the steps a layer draws behind one arrow on the core map. Draw it in one direction, from its first variable to its last, and read it the way a loop is read: each minus sign turns the direction. An even count of minus signs means the end moves with the start, and an odd count means it moves the other way.

Our systems atlas holds its chains to this: “Where the core map draws one arrow for a longer chain, the economy and technology layers show the steps, and their combined sign agrees with the core arrow.” Where a page shows a chain and the core arrow it stands behind, draw the core arrow beside the chain.

text: A reader who takes the last step’s sign as the chain’s answer will often get it backward. Here the last step raises households’ financial security, and the chain as a whole lowers it, as the core arrow says.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s model conventions

correct.caption: An open chain from our systems atlas through its economy layer, read with its signs carried along, beside connection L37, the core map’s one arrow for the same path.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.8. The summary arrow takes the last step’s plus, so the chain reads as raising households’ financial security. One minus sign along the way turns it, as connection L37 says.

specs.label: Direction
specs.value: One way, first variable to last; an open chain never bends back into a loop

specs.label: Combined sign
specs.value: An even count of minus signs for the same direction, odd for the opposite

specs.label: Core arrow
specs.value: Beside the chain where the page shows both, with its own sign

specs.label: Read aloud
specs.value: More or less at each variable, carrying the signs, as Rule 15.6 reads a loop

builders: Work out the combined sign by script from each connection’s record, and stop the build if it disagrees with the core arrow.

rules.title: Frame the atlas’s layers and clusters, and set outside drivers beyond the frames.
rule: Our systems atlas sorts its 51 variables into three layers: the core, “Power and accountability”, with 31 variables, five of them outside drivers and the rest in five clusters; the economy layer, with 12; and the technology layer, with eight. Where a drawing shows variables from more than one layer, name each layer and mark its edge with a 1 px rule: a frame around each, one rule between two layers that stack, with both names, or a box around a layer that sits inside a drawing of another. Name the cluster of a core variable where the drawing frames it.

An outside driver is “a force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary”, in the atlas’s words. Set it outside every frame, with its kind in words. Where a connection crosses a frame, break the frame around the line, so a reader sees where the effect comes in.

text: The frames tell a reader what the model explains and what it takes as given. A driver drawn inside a cluster reads as one more thing the model accounts for, and the atlas treats its five drivers as given from 2026 to 2036.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s layers, boundary and glossary

correct.caption: Foreign interference outside every frame, exposure to hostile political content in the core layer’s cluster B, and feed ranking in the technology layer, with each frame broken where a connection crosses it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.9. Foreign interference sits inside the model’s frame as one more variable, and feed ranking loses its layer, so a reader cannot tell what the model explains.

specs.label: Frame
specs.value: 1 px in the strong border color, its name at top right inside, 15 px

specs.label: Two layers
specs.value: One 1 px rule between them with both names at its right end, or a box around the smaller

specs.label: Crossing
specs.value: The frame breaks 7 px each side of the line

specs.label: Outside driver
specs.value: Outside every frame, marked Outside driver; the atlas’s glossary draws it as a rounded pill

specs.label: Layers
specs.value: Core 31, economy 12, technology 8; core clusters A to E

builders: Read each variable’s layer and cluster from the atlas’s layers record, and break a frame wherever a connection’s line crosses it.

rules.title: Show what the model leaves out beside what it draws.
rule: Our systems atlas keeps a record of what it left off its map: three connections it reviewed against the evidence and did not draw, nine subjects it names as omitted, and a boundary that lists what the model does not cover. Where a drawing shows a mechanism next to one of those connections, print the connection beside it in words, with the atlas’s reason, under the heading Reviewed and not drawn.
Draw no line for a connection the atlas reviewed and left out, in any pattern.

text: A reader who sees feed ranking raise hostile content will ask whether feed ranking raises hostility itself. The atlas reviewed that claim and left it off its map, and its reason answers the question with the evidence.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s rejected connections, omissions and limits

correct.caption: Connection LT01 from our systems atlas, with the connection the atlas reviewed and left off its map printed beside it in words, with the atlas’s reason.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.10. A dashed line runs from feed ranking to hostility toward the other party, a connection the atlas reviewed and left off its map, so the drawing claims some evidence where the largest experiments found no measurable change.

specs.label: Heading
specs.value: Reviewed and not drawn

specs.label: Words
specs.value: From and to, with typed chips, and the atlas’s reason quoted

specs.label: Line
specs.value: None, in any pattern

specs.label: Records
specs.value: Three rejected connections and nine omissions, as of the snapshot

builders: Look up the atlas’s rejected connections for every pair of variables a drawing shows, and print any match in words beside the drawing.

rules.title: Place a reform on the exact connections and variables it targets, with its band.
rule: Each of our systems atlas’s 50 reforms lists its targets, the exact connections and variables it acts on, and the loops it sits on. Draw the reform on a drawing that holds its targets, and turn only those marks red, as Rule 12.5 sets: each target connection with its arrowhead, and the outline of each target variable. Beside the drawing, name the reform, say that it acts where the marks turn red, and list each target in its typed chip.

Mark the targets one by one, even where they fill a cluster, and never turn a frame, a cluster or a whole loop red in their place. Print the reform’s band, the kind of change it makes, beside it in the atlas’s words. The bands follow Donella Meadows’ ordering of places to intervene in a system, from changing a number to changing what the system aims for. Of the 50 reforms, 26 change rules, 11 change a parameter, five feedback, four information, three the power to change the rules and one goals.

text: A reform acts on a few connections and variables, and the rest of the mechanism has to respond on its own. Red on the exact targets shows a reader where the reform acts, before any claim about results. Red on a whole cluster says it acts on variables the atlas never lists.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s reform profiles and its bands of change; Rule 12.5

correct.caption: Reform R-03 on Loop R4a, with red on its one connection and two variables and nothing else, its targets listed in typed chips and its band in the atlas’s words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.11. The red follows the electoral competition cluster, so Variable C4 reads as a target and Variable D7, which the atlas lists, stays in ink.

specs.label: Targets
specs.value: Only the connections and variables the reform’s record lists, in Rule 12.5’s red: a connection at 4 px on its ink edge, with its arrowhead; a variable’s outline at 3 px

specs.label: Never red
specs.value: A frame, a cluster or a whole loop in place of the targets

specs.label: Note
specs.value: The reform’s chip and the words “acts where the marks turn red”, with the count of each kind

specs.label: Band
specs.value: The atlas’s word and its definition, quoted: parameter, feedback, information, rules, power to change the rules or goals

specs.label: Loops
specs.value: Each loop the reform sits on, in its typed chip; the drawing shows one that holds every target

builders: Read the targets, loops and band from the reform’s own record, set the red only on marks whose IDs the record lists, and stop the build if a red mark carries any other ID.

rules.title: Grade the evidence for the problem and for the remedy apart.
rule: Our systems atlas grades each reform twice. In its glossary’s words, evidence of the problem is “evidence that the condition or mechanism a reform addresses exists”, and evidence for the remedy is “evidence that an intervention changes the condition it targets”. Print each as its own label with Rule 13.3’s word and gloss, and quote the atlas’s words under it.

A drawing of the reform carries a third grade, how sure the atlas is of the mechanism. Each connection shows it in its line code, the solid, dashed or dotted line Rule 13.4 sets by grade. Print each connection’s grade word in the list of steps under the drawing, and keep all three grades apart. Of the atlas’s 50 reforms, 49 carry two different grades, and in 48 of them the remedy’s grade is the lower.

text: A problem on the record says nothing yet about whether a fix works. A reader shown one grade carries the stronger to both, and a well-documented harm then reads as proof of an untested remedy.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary and reform profiles; Rule 13.3

correct.caption: Reform R-32 with its two grades apart: the evidence of the problem well supported, and the evidence for the remedy a hypothesis, each in the atlas’s words, with each connection’s grade in the list of steps under the drawing.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.12. One label, Well supported, covers the reform, so the loss of local news reads as proof that funding would restore it. The atlas grades that remedy a hypothesis.

specs.label: Problem
specs.value: Its own label: Rule 13.3’s word and gloss, then “evidence of the problem”, and the atlas’s words quoted

specs.label: Remedy
specs.value: Its own label the same way, “evidence for the remedy”

specs.label: Order
specs.value: The problem’s label first and the remedy’s second, as the first two labels on the plate

specs.label: Connections
specs.value: Their own line code (Rule 13.4), and each one’s grade word in the list of steps under the drawing

specs.label: Never
specs.value: One grade for the whole reform

specs.label: Counts
specs.value: 49 of 50 reforms carry two different grades, as of the snapshot

builders: Read the two grades from problem_evidence and remedy_evidence, print each through Rule 13.3’s table, and never fall back from one to the other.

rules.title: Let the least certain step set how far a reader trusts a loop.
rule: Loop R1, “Wealth and political influence reinforce each other”, runs through three connections that carry money. Two are well supported. The middle one, connection L02, “Political spending can tilt policy toward donors”, is plausible, and our systems atlas names it the weakest step. The loop as a whole takes that grade: the atlas grades Loop R1 plausible.

Draw each step in its own line, mark the weakest in words, and give the diagram’s label the grade of the least certain step (Rule 13.1). The loop stepper of Rule 18.22 runs the same loop live, one connection at a time, in Rule 11.14’s plate.

text: A loop runs only when each of its steps runs, so its least certain step limits the whole. A reader who sees two solid lines and one dashed line can say how far the loop holds before reading its record.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, the record and evidence summary of Loop R1

correct.caption: Loop R1 from our systems atlas, with its middle step dashed and marked as the weakest, under a label that gives the whole loop that step’s grade.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.13. Every step is solid and the label reads Well supported, so the loop borrows the grade of its strongest steps and hides the one the atlas calls weakest.

specs.label: Each step
specs.value: Its own line, by its own grade (Rule 13.4)

specs.label: Weakest step
specs.value: “Weakest step” under its words, where the atlas’s evidence summary names it

specs.label: The loop’s label
specs.value: The least certain step’s grade (Rule 13.1)

specs.label: Live
specs.value: The loop stepper of Rule 18.22 runs Loop R1 in Rule 11.14’s plate

builders: Take the weakest step from the loop’s evidence summary and the label from the least certain connection, and stop the build if the two disagree.

rules.title: Show a change to the model in the atlas’s own words, with its date.
rule: Our systems atlas revises its model as the evidence changes, and it records some revisions in its own text. Loop R8, “Housing scarcity strengthens owners’ incentive to restrict building”, carries one: its evidence note reads “well-supported for both links”, and says the loop “no longer depends on” Variable A1, concentration of household wealth. Quote a revision as the atlas writes it, with the snapshot date, and draw the loop as it stands now.
A drawing made before the revision is a record of what we drew. It is never evidence for the model, and a page that published one corrects it as Rule 13.13 sets out.

text: A revision in the atlas’s own words lets a reader check it against the atlas, and the date tells them which version they read. This one changes what the loop explains: the atlas records that rising home equity tends to lower the top wealth share, so the loop no longer accounts for wealth at the top.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, the record of Loop R8 and Connection T12

correct.caption: Loop R8 as our systems atlas holds it, with the atlas’s revision and its reason quoted beside the drawing, as of October 15, 2026.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.14. The drawing routes Loop R8 through concentration of household wealth with plus signs and prints no date. The atlas says the loop no longer depends on Variable A1, and its connection T12 runs from home equity to the top wealth share with a minus.

specs.label: Revision
specs.value: The atlas’s words, quoted, from the record that carries them

specs.label: Date
specs.value: “As of” and the snapshot date, October 15, 2026 (Rule 13.10)

specs.label: Drawing
specs.value: The loop as the atlas holds it now

specs.label: An earlier drawing
specs.value: A record, never evidence; a published one is corrected under Rule 13.13

builders: Quote the revision from the loop’s own fields, and stop the build when those fields change, so the quotation never drifts from the atlas.

rules.title: Follow a variable two loops share through each loop in turn.
rule: Loop B4, “Electoral consequences can improve public performance”, and Loop R10, “Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates”, both pass through Variable C3, risk of losing office. Draw the two loops side by side, give the shared variable its own title in both, and fill its pill in ink in each drawing, the one place a pill takes a fill. Under each loop, print the connection that brings a change into the shared variable and the one that carries it on, with the atlas’s sentence on each sign.

Then say where the loops meet, in the atlas’s words. As primaries decide more seats in Loop R10, the risk of losing office falls, and in Loop B4 that same risk turns poor service into defeats that improve it. The atlas says Loop B4 “works only where seats are competitive”.

text: Two loops drawn apart look like two separate stories. A variable they share is where one can weaken or strengthen the other, and a reader can find it only if it carries one name and one mark in both.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, Loops B4 and R10 and the glossary entry “Electoral pressure”

correct.caption: Loop B4 beside Loop R10, with Variable C3 filled in ink in both, the connections in and out of it in each loop, and the atlas’s words on where the two meet.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.15. The shared variable takes a different name in each loop and no mark, so the loops read as unrelated. Both pass through Variable C3, the risk of losing office.

specs.label: Order
specs.value: The two loops side by side from 680 px, one under the other below it

specs.label: Shared variable
specs.value: Its own title in both drawings, its pill filled in ink with its name in the surface color

specs.label: In and out
specs.value: Under each loop, the connection into the shared variable and the one out of it, with their chips, grade words and the atlas’s sentences on their signs

specs.label: Where they meet
specs.value: The atlas’s words, quoted, with the shared variable’s chip

builders: Find the shared variable as the overlap of the two loops’ chains, by script, and stop the build if the loops share none or more than the one the page follows.

rules.title: Show a reform’s four effects apart, with each route’s check date.
rule: Reform R-01, “All-party primaries with ranked general elections”, targets two connections and one variable on Loop R10, and sits on Loops R10, B4 and R11. Draw it where it acts (Rule 15.11), then print its effects one outcome family to a row, each with the atlas’s code, its words and the pips of Rule 13.5, and no row that adds them. Its routes follow, each with who acts there, its feasibility and its own check date, or “Not checked” where the atlas gives none (Rule 13.10).

As of October 15, 2026, the atlas codes its effect on the quality of democracy moderate positive, on government efficacy small positive, and on the other two families no expected effect. It checked the state ballot and local routes on that date, and the state statute and federal statute routes carry no date.

text: A single score would hide what the atlas keeps apart: the families use different units, and a reform can help one while it costs another. A route rated without a date reads as current, and a reader deciding where to act needs to know which ratings the atlas checked.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, the profile of Reform R-01 and the note on effect codes; Rules 13.5 and 13.10

correct.caption: Reform R-01 at its targets on Loop R10, with its four effects one family to a row and its four routes each dated or marked not checked, as of October 15, 2026.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.16. The card adds two gains into one large positive score and dates all four routes October 15, 2026. The atlas adds no families, and it checked only the ballot and local routes.

specs.label: Where it acts
specs.value: Its targets in Rule 12.5’s red, as Rule 15.11 sets

specs.label: Effects
specs.value: One row per outcome family, in the atlas’s order, with the pips, the code and its words; the atlas’s note that codes are never added, quoted

specs.label: Routes
specs.value: Chip and name, who acts, feasibility, and “Checked” with the route’s own date, or “Not checked”

specs.label: Date
specs.value: “As of October 15, 2026” over the effects, the snapshot date

specs.label: Never
specs.value: A total, an overall score, or a route dated from the reform’s status

builders: Print each family from the reform’s effects record and each route from its routes list, and stop the build if any row sums or a route without a checked date prints one.

rules.title: Draw who holds power over each layer in one authority diagram.
rule: Our systems atlas records seven authority connections. Each runs from a variable in the core layer that holds a body’s power, such as Congress’s ability to write and check policy, to a variable in the economy or technology layer that the body has the legal power to set. Draw all seven in one diagram: the layers stacked with a rule between each and its name, one pill for each variable, carrying the variable’s own title, and every line in the authority mark of Rule 15.5. Name each body beside the diagram as the atlas’s connections name it. Every line in it means the same verb, decides, so print the word once, in a key beside the diagram.

Run the lines into each layer in lanes on one side of the column, nested so that none crosses another, and list each connection beside the diagram with its name. Then a reader sees what no single line shows: three of the four variables each answer to two bodies, and Congress and the executive each reach both layers.

text: Power in the atlas is shared. Congress appropriates public investment and the executive administers it; antitrust enforcers set rules for pricing software, and so do states and cities. One diagram keeps every body apart and shows where their powers meet.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s authority connections and model conventions

correct.caption: The atlas’s seven authority connections in one diagram, from the powers of four bodies in the core layer to four variables in the economy and technology layers, with each body and each connection named beside it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.17. One pill for the government stands in for four bodies, so the drawing cannot say who decides what. The atlas records four apart: Congress, the executive, antitrust enforcers, and state and local governments.

specs.label: Layers
specs.value: Stacked, with one 1 px rule between each two and both names beside it (Rule 15.9)

specs.label: Bodies
specs.value: One pill for the variable that holds each body’s power, in the core layer, carrying the variable’s own title; the body’s plain name beside the diagram, as the atlas’s connections give it

specs.label: Lines
specs.value: The authority mark of Rule 15.5: solid, an open diamond, no sign, with its delay ticks

specs.label: Key
specs.value: Two entries: decides, printed once because every line in the diagram means the same, and the delay ticks (Rule 13.5); each connection’s name beside the diagram says who decides what

specs.label: Lanes
specs.value: Lines into the economy layer on the right and into the technology layer on the left, 12 px apart, nested so none crosses

specs.label: Beside it
specs.value: Each connection’s chip, name and grade word, grouped by the layer it reaches

builders: Read every authority connection from the atlas, check that each runs from the core layer and sits in no loop, and stop the build if the count or any end changes.

rules.title: Print a conceptual loop’s missing chain beside its grade.
rule: Loop B2, “Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks”, is one of our systems atlas’s three conceptual loops. The atlas grades its mechanism well supported, and none of its steps is a numbered connection. Draw it as Rule 15.7 sets, with hollow lines between thin pills, and print in the label, right after the grade, that the loop has no numbered chain and that the atlas calls this its weakest point.

Quote the atlas’s words on the missing chain beside the drawing, tie each station to a numbered variable where the atlas does, and name the atlas’s other conceptual loops, Loop B3 and Loop R9, with their grades.

text: A grade printed alone reads as the grade of each step. For a conceptual loop it belongs to the mechanism as a whole, and no step carries a citation of its own, so a reader cannot check the loop one step at a time.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, the record and evidence summary of Loop B2

correct.caption: Loop B2 with its missing chain in the label beside its grade, the atlas’s words on it, and the atlas’s other two conceptual loops named with their grades.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.18. The label gives the grade alone, so Well supported reads as a checked chain of steps. The atlas grades the mechanism and calls the missing chain its weakest point.

specs.label: Label
specs.value: The grade word, then “no numbered chain”, in one line

specs.label: Drawing
specs.value: Hollow lines with their signs, 1 px pills, no step numbers (Rule 15.7)

specs.label: Beside it
specs.value: The atlas’s words on the missing chain, quoted; a station tied to a numbered variable in its chip

specs.label: The others
specs.value: Each conceptual loop named in its chip with its grade; three as of the snapshot

builders: Read the closure and the evidence summary from the loop’s record, and stop the build if a conceptual loop gains numbered connections or the summary changes.

rules.title: Step a reader through a loop one connection at a time, with a still sequence.
rule: Let a reader move through a loop one connection at a time, in the loop’s own order, with Play, Pause, Reset the loop, Previous step and Next step, since a loop read all at once asks a reader to hold every step in mind. Use the loop stepper of Rule 18.22, its markup and its code, and set the drawing beside it so the current step lights in both.

Each step’s words say everything the drawing shows for it: the two variables by their own titles, which way the change runs, what moves along the connection, its grade and its delay. Number every step, and print the whole sequence in order wherever nothing can move: on paper, with motion reduced and with scripts off.

text: A stepper adds the loop’s order to the shape its drawing shows. When a reader takes the loop one connection at a time, the weakest step stands out where it falls, and the reader sees why the loop’s grade is that step’s grade (Rule 15.13). The still sequence keeps the same reading for a reader who cannot or will not run it.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, Loop R1; the stepper and still-sequence lessons of LOOPY, as Rule 18.22 sets them

correct.caption: Loop R1, where wealth and political influence reinforce each other, on the loop stepper of Rule 18.22, live: three numbered steps, each with its connection, grade and delay. The current step lights in the drawing and in the list; on paper and with scripts off the list shows every step in order.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.19. The player shows one step at a time and nothing else: no numbers, no list and no way to pause, so on paper, with motion reduced or with scripts off a reader sees one connection of three.

specs.label: Component
specs.value: The loop stepper of Rule 18.22: its markup, its styles and its script, once on the page

specs.label: Current step
specs.value: The selected band behind its line and its two pills, the list’s band and bar beside it, in ink, never in red

specs.label: Steps ahead
specs.value: Muted, each line keeping its grade’s pattern

specs.label: Step words
specs.value: The variables’ titles and the sign’s verb, then the connection, what moves along it, its grade and its delay

specs.label: Still sequence
specs.value: Every step numbered and in ink, buttons hidden, on paper, with motion reduced and with scripts off

builders: Carry Rule 18.22’s markup and let chapter 18’s script run it; never copy the script. Light the drawing from the stepper’s data-oa-at, and number the steps with a CSS counter, never inside the line the status reads.

rules.title: Let a reader choose a reform and see its targets, effects and assumptions.
rule: Offer the reforms that act on one drawing as a named group of radio buttons (Rule 18.3), so a reader chooses one at a time. The chosen reform’s exact targets turn red on the drawing (Rule 15.11), and its panel lists its targets, its band, its four effects apart in the atlas’s codes with their date (Rule 15.16) and its routes, each with its check date or “Not checked”.

Keep the atlas’s qualifications and assumptions one step away, in a disclosure under the panel (Rule 18.8), and never light two reforms at once or add their effects. Offer only reforms whose every target sits on the drawing, so nothing lights for a reform that does not act there.

text: A reader comparing reforms wants to see where each one acts and what the atlas expects of it. One choice at a time keeps each reform’s red its own, and the effects stay the atlas’s four ordinal codes. The assumptions sit one step away, where a reader who asks finds them whole.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, Reforms R-03 and R-04 on Loop R4a; the choice lessons of En-ROADS, as Rules 18.3 and 18.8 set them

correct.caption: Reform R-03, proportional elections in multi-seat House districts, and Reform R-04, independent citizen commissions that draw election maps, on Loop R4a, where majorities draw maps that help them keep control, live: choose one and its targets turn red, with its effects and routes beside the drawing and its qualifications one step away.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.20. Both reforms light at once, so no red says whose target it is, and a combined score adds effects our systems atlas never adds. The qualifications are gone.

specs.label: Choice
specs.value: A named group of radio buttons, two to five reforms, the first chosen on load (Rule 18.3)

specs.label: Targets
specs.value: The chosen reform’s alone, in Rule 12.5’s red, with each named in a typed chip

specs.label: Effects
specs.value: Four rows, one outcome family each, in the atlas’s codes with their date; never added

specs.label: Assumptions
specs.value: In a disclosure under the panel, closed on load, open on paper (Rule 18.8)

specs.label: Status line
specs.value: One sentence on each change, hidden from sight, never on load

builders: Show the chosen panel and light its targets from the checked radio with CSS, so the choice works with scripts off; let the shell’s listener write the status line from the panel’s first line.

rules.title: Give every control the model’s own steps, and no slider for a strength.
rule: A control may offer only what the model holds: its loops and their steps, its reforms, Rule 13.3’s grade words, the three delay classes and the four ordinal effect codes. Each is a set of named steps, so build it from the stepper, the radio group or the disclosure.

Leave totals, odds, amounts and strengths out of every control, and with them sliders, dials and fields for a number, because our systems atlas leaves the size of any effect to the studies behind each connection and says that “no whole loop has a measured strength.” A slider set between 0 and 100 would hand a reader a figure no study supports.

text: A slider promises that any value along it means something and that moving it changes the outcome by that much. The atlas grades its connections in words and codes its effects in ordinal steps, so the honest control offers those steps alone.
why.basis: Our systems atlas, Connection L55 and the model’s limits

correct.caption: Connection L55, “Safe seats keep majorities in power”, with what our systems atlas holds for it, each on the model’s own steps: its sign, its grade on the ladder, its delay class, and no strength.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 15.21. A slider sets the connection’s strength at 70 of 100, a figure our systems atlas does not hold. A line under the slider says the picture made the value up.

specs.label: Steps a control may offer
specs.value: Loops and their steps, reforms, grade words, delay classes and ordinal effect codes

specs.label: Never offered
specs.value: A total, odds, an amount or a strength, whether by slider, dial or number field

specs.label: A picture of a control
specs.value: Drawn, not built, with its alt saying it is a picture

builders: Stop the build if a plate or a control prints a number the model’s record does not hold.
